newsitem.title: USA: U.S. economy growing, some pockets of weakness-Fed.
newsitem.headline: U.S. economy growing, some pockets of weakness-Fed.

text.p: The economy grew across the country in May and early June but showed some pockets of weakness including slower growth in consumer spending, the Federal Reserve said on Wednesday.
Labor markets tightened but there was little or no wage pressure. There were few price hikes reported, except for energy and real estate, the Fed said.

"All 12 district economies expanded in May and early June, although there were pockets of weakness and evidence of capacity constraints restraining growth in some industries," the Fed's Beige Book summary said.
The summary was prepared by the Dallas Fed, one of 12 regional banks, based on information collected before June 9.
It will be used by policysetting members of the central bank's Federal Open Market Committree when they meet July 1-2 to consider interest-rate strategy.

The summary noted that consumer spending growth slowed in May and June from the pace that was reported in the last Beige Book summary issued on May 7. Several districts said retail and auto sales were slower and some reported unwanted inventory buildups.
"Labor markets tightened, leading to some wage increases," the Fed summary said, though it noted later that there was "little or no wage pressure" overall.

It said labor markets continued to be tight for skilled professionals in high-tech, construction and energy industries. Businesses in a number of districts said they were having more difficulty finding blue-collar and entry-level workers as well.
Manufacturing activity was brisk and growing in most districts. There were some areas of weakness though only Atlanta said overall production was slowing.
The Fed summary said strong demand for steel and heavy equipment led to rising production in the Chicago area and that capacity utilization "remained very high" in the region.
Businesses in the Chicago, Dallas, New York and Philadelphia Fed bank regions all said manufacturing activity was continuing to expand.

While prices were higher for energy, some metals and for real estate, there was little pressure on final prices. The summary said "retail and manufacturing prices were being held in check by heavy competition, which was stimulating continued cost reduction or productivity increases."

The summary said that housing, construction and land prices were increasing. It noted "sharp rises" in New York City co-op and condo prices and a 20 percent hike in Dallas office rents from a year earlier.

Banks described lending as mixed, with stronger demand for commercial than for consumer loans. Competition was stiff for business loans, keeping interest rates down and leading to more relaxed credit requirements in several Fed regions including Chicago, Dallas and St Louis, the Fed summary said.
